chief_complaint: burning pain down back of right leg to ankle, SLR positive
hpi_details: A 20-year-old female presents to the clinic with burning pain down back of right leg to ankle, slr positive. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks she pulled a deep hamstring tendon or strained a nerve while carrying heavy storage boxes into her apartment.
concerns: She is worried that the burning pain will make it impossible for her to sit through her upcoming university midterm exams.
expectations: She hopes to get effective pain medication to quiet the burning and a medical accommodation note for standing breaks during classes.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Lumbar Radiculopathy (Sciatica) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for S1 Lower Back Sciatica: McKenzie extension exercises, core stabilization, oral NSAIDs, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Lumbar Radiculopathy (Sciatica).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Lumbar spinal stenosis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Cauda equina syndrome (saddle anesthesia, bowel/bladder incontinence).

reference_soap.plan: For suspected S1 lumbar radiculopathy, use guided extension exercises and core stabilization; consider oral NSAIDs only when clinically appropriate and not contraindicated. Arrange prompt assessment for worsening weakness and emergency evaluation for saddle numbness or bowel/bladder changes; consider specialist review for persistent symptoms. Counsel the patient.

must_ask.say: Does the pain shoot down past your knee into your foot or toes?
Does coughing, sneezing, or sitting down make the leg pain much worse?
Have you noticed any numbness around your buttocks or loss of bowel or bladder control?
Does raising your straight leg while lying flat trigger the shooting pain?
Do you feel weakness when walking on your heels or toes?

history.answer: I came in because I have a burning pain running down the back of my right leg all the way to my ankle.
The burning starts in my right buttock and shoots straight down the back of my thigh, through my calf, and into my outer ankle and foot.
It started about five days ago after I helped my roommate move several heavy storage boxes, and it has been gradually getting worse.
It feels like a sharp, burning, and electric-like pain, and at its worst it reaches about a 7 out of 10.
Sitting down for long periods, bending forward, or coughing and sneezing makes the shooting pain much sharper. Lying flat with a pillow under my knees eases it slightly.
If I find the right position in bed it settles down, but tossing or turning at night triggers a sharp jolt that wakes me up.
history.topic: Pain at rest and night pain

history.answer: I don't have morning stiffness lasting more than a few minutes, and moving around doesn't make the pain better like it would with inflammatory arthritis.
Yes, I have numbness and a pins-and-needles feeling along the outer border and bottom of my right foot.
My right foot feels slightly clumsy, and I notice I have difficulty pushing off or standing up on my right tiptoes.
No, I have normal bladder and bowel control with no leakage, urgency, or retention.
No, the sensation around my groin, buttocks, and between my legs feels completely normal.
I don't get cramping in both calves that forces me to stop walking, and sitting down actually makes my pain worse rather than relieving it.
No fever, chills, or night sweats, but I have felt generally run-down and fatigued since the pain started.
No, I have never had cancer.
No recent infections, no spine injections or procedures, no diabetes, and I have never used intravenous drugs.
No, I don't have osteoporosis, I've never taken steroid medications, and I haven't had any high-impact falls.
No stomach pain, no burning or blood in my urine, and no pulsing sensations in my abdomen.
No eye redness or pain, no heel pain, no chronic diarrhea, and no scaly skin patches.
Yesterday while lying down I tried raising my straight right leg into the air, and it triggered an intense electric shock straight down to my ankle.
I took some over-the-counter ibuprofen a couple of times, but it only dulled the ache slightly and didn't stop the burning.
I am a university student, so I spend long hours sitting at a desk studying, which has been aggravating the pain.
I thought I must have badly pulled a hamstring tendon or strained something deep in my leg when I was carrying heavy boxes up the stairs.
I'm really worried that this burning pain will make it impossible for me to sit through my two-hour midterm exams next week.
I'm hoping to get some strong medicine to calm the burning down, and maybe a doctor's note so my professors let me stand up and stretch during lectures.
I have always been healthy and have no chronic medical conditions.
I have never had surgery and have never been hospitalized.
I don't take any regular prescription medications or supplements, just the ibuprofen I tried recently.
I don't have any allergies to medications or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
I only drink socially, maybe one drink once or twice a month.
Both of my parents are healthy, and there is no family history of spine surgery or nerve disorders.
My last period was about two weeks ago and my cycles are regular. There is no chance of pregnancy, and I am not currently sexually active.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 115/75 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, body temperature 36.6°C, SpO2 99% on room air.

Mild tenderness over the right lumbosacral paraspinal musculature; right straight-leg raise test is positive at 40 degrees reproducing the sharp burning pain down to the lateral ankle, while left straight-leg raise is negative.
Decreased pinprick and light touch sensation along the right lateral foot and plantar surface, consistent with the S1 dermatome.
Right ankle plantarflexion strength is reduced to 4/5, while knee extension, knee flexion, ankle dorsiflexion, and great toe extension are intact at 5/5 bilaterally.
Right Achilles deep tendon reflex is diminished (1+) compared to normal (2+) on the left; patellar reflexes are symmetric and plantar responses are flexor bilaterally.
Antalgic gait favoring the right lower extremity, with inability to perform repetitive single-leg heel rises on the right.
Normal resting anal sphincter tone, intact voluntary contraction, and normal perianal sensation.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender throughout, and without palpable pulsatile masses or organomegaly.
No costovertebral angle tenderness elicited bilaterally.
